lede: Dewey answers questions about dblp by calling tools over the whole dump, including its own index of 5.49 million abstracts of dblp's papers. This study measures it against RAGScholar, the retrieval system DBLP-QA was built for, on RAGScholar's own kind of question and on questions about dblp's records. Every answer is graded automatically and repeatably, by two judges from different model families.

findings.title: Answering is solved; finding is not
findings.text: Given the abstract a question was written from, gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini and Mistral-7B all score at least 1.96 of 2. Re-running the original study's ten ways of building the context reproduces its ordering (rank correlation 0.92 for Mistral-7B), but what separates systems now is whether retrieval finds the paper.

findings.title: An open index replaces the closed one
findings.text: RAGScholar's index of 4.6 million abstracts cannot be rebuilt. Dewey's index, read from OpenAlex's open snapshot in under two hours, holds 5.49 million abstracts of dblp's papers and the source abstract of 90% of DBLP-QA's questions. Alone it puts the right paper in the top five for 68% of them, against 58% for the best pipeline over four live search services.

findings.title: On held-out questions, Dewey matches or beats RAGScholar
findings.text: On 100 questions about 2025–2026 papers, built only after Dewey's design was frozen, Dewey scores 1.74 against 0.89 without retrieval. RAGScholar's best configuration scores 1.73 when it reads candidates gathered offline from three search services and 1.63 on Dewey's open index (Dewey better on 12 questions, worse on 2), a margin owed partly to Dewey's stronger writing model. Under the second judge, Dewey's lead is significant on both the held-out set and DBLP-QA.

findings.title: Dewey's live search is as good as the offline pool
findings.text: Given the fixed pipeline's own candidates, which show the source with the very abstract the question was written from, Dewey scores 1.75; searching for itself, in seconds, 1.74. The best fixed pipeline, gpt-4.1-mini on those candidates, scores 1.80: within noise of Dewey on the held-out set, but 0.09 ahead over all 300 newer questions.

findings.title: A bibliography is asked more than what papers say
findings.text: On 70 questions about dblp's records, such as how many papers a venue published in a year or how many people share a name, scored by exact match against values computed from the dump, Dewey answers 65 and a RAGScholar-style pipeline 20: five retrieved records cannot be counted, ranked or told apart.

findings.title: It is the grading, not the wrong papers
findings.text: Graded against the one reference answer, retrieving the wrong papers seems to cost points. Graded so that any correct answer counts, after controls, neither judge finds a measurable cost: the models give different correct answers, not wrong ones.

dewey_title: How Dewey answers what papers say
dewey: Dewey's abstract search runs four searches at once: its own index of 5.49 million abstracts (BM25, about 75 milliseconds), its hybrid search over every dblp title, and OpenAlex's keyword and semantic search. It keeps the papers dblp has, ranks them, and fuses that ranking with the index's own; a paper newer than the index keeps its live rank, so recency is never a penalty.

The five best abstracts go to gpt-4.1, which answers from the one that addresses the question most directly and cites every sentence as [1] to [5]. On the held-out questions Dewey searched every time, gave the right abstract to its writer on 85 of 100 and cited its sources in 98 answers, never citing an abstract it was not shown.
The study's evaluation harness lives in the same codebase as Dewey and runs on the same machine, so every later version of Dewey is measured the same way.
